title: What Stayed
encoding: WebP quality94 from generated PNG, without resize or composition changes
sourceCredit: This American Life, Episode 541, “Regrets, I’ve Had a Few”
sourceNotes: Compilation of different accounts, NOT one person; segment provenance and credits need verification before release.
imagePrompt: Create one landscape 1536 x 1024 production sprite atlas: exactly TWO columns and THREE rows, six wide cinematic full-scene panels in row-major order 0,1 / 2,3 / 4,5. Each cell fills approximately 768 x 341 pixels (last row 342), flush edge to edge, no gutters or borders. Every cell is a standalone wide composition, not a square image pasted on a wide matte. Painterly literary motion-comic art: watercolor pigment, restrained ink contours, colored-pencil texture, natural anatomy, coherent perspective, grounded feet, credible hands, soft practical light. Keep faces and essential hand/object contact comfortably inside the cell. Show seated bodies joined naturally to chair and table; include chair seats, knees, ankles and shoes when visible. No detached limbs, paper-doll joints, rigid mannequin poses, extra fingers or floating props. Keep cast, clothing, anatomy, furniture and setting consistent across relevant cells. These are fictional adaptation illustrations, not portraits or photographs of real source subjects. NO lettering, labels, logos, readable writing, panel numbers, captions, speech text or watermarks anywhere. Chapter: What Stayed. Cast/design continuity: Three unrelated fictional accounts with distinct people and settings. CHILD: small dark-curly-haired girl in a faded brick-red cardigan in a domestic hallway with a broom. ADULT: stocky bearded man with shaved head, grey rolled-sleeve shirt in a quiet clinic waiting/appointment room; any old arm marking is obscured and never identifiable. WALKER: slender middle-aged man with straight brown hair, olive coat and worn brown shoes at a park bench. No shared family, crossover, hateful symbols or invented cure.. CELL 0: CHILD ONLY, first unrelated account. A curly-haired girl in brick-red cardigan stands in a quiet domestic hallway beside a broom leaning against the wall. Her hands hold each other uneasily and she glances toward someone entirely offscreen. The broom casts one long ordinary shadow. No tattooed adult or walker appears. CELL 1: CHILD ONLY, same independent hallway and girl. She lowers her gaze and lets one hand fall from the other, still uneasy after a partial admission; broom and its shadow remain. Do not add a confession, punishment, happy absolution or age transition. No other account’s person or object enters. CELL 2: ADULT ONLY, second unrelated account. A stocky shaved-headed bearded man in a grey rolled-sleeve shirt sits at a quiet clinic appointment table, turning his own forearm upward and looking at it with sober responsibility. The old marking is covered by a plain gauze area or indistinct neutral patch; no hateful emblem, readable tattoo, blood or child from the first account. CELL 3: ADULT ONLY, same distinct bearded man at a quiet clinic chair, forearm supported comfortably on an armrest, free hand relaxed in his lap while he waits. Plain appointment environment, no active procedure, medical spectacle, instant erasure or redemption effect. The shoe-walker is not this man. CELL 4: WALKER ONLY, third unrelated account. Slender straight-brown-haired man in olive coat sits on a park bench, one shoe removed and supported in his hands as he feels along its interior lining. His socked foot rests safely on the ground; the other shoe stays on. No tattoo, clinic, broom or child; small physical irritation at its own scale. CELL 5: WALKER ONLY, same park and distinct man. Both worn brown shoes are now on; he rises from the bench and takes one small step, pausing as discomfort remains. One hand releases the bench edge, body naturally balanced. No discovered object, cure, dramatic injury or moral resolution. Editorial limit: Two dedicated scenes for each unrelated account. The childhood lie, responsibility for hateful ink and walker’s minor irritation are not one life. No hateful mark is rendered. Linking narration is not assigned to any pictured protagonist; no unprovided confession or cure.
layoutNotes: Collective opening, time-transition and closing beats use three separated wide panels, with a dedicated panel for each independent life. Individual dialogue stays in that person’s full-size scene.
